steps.title: North of Cape Town
steps.body: Swartland, black land, lies about 65 km north of Cape Town, named after the dark renosterbos shrub that covers its hills. It's a large area of wheat fields and vineyards, around towns like Malmesbury and Riebeek-Kasteel, with the Paardeberg and Kasteelberg mountains. Soils include granite, schist and iron-rich clay.

steps.title: Hot and dry
steps.body: Swartland is warmer and drier than Stellenbosch, with hot summers and about 300 to 600 mm of rain a year, mostly in winter. Many vines are bush vines, dry-farmed without irrigation, their deep roots finding water. That keeps yields low and fruit concentrated. Atlantic breezes cool some western areas.

options: Dry-farmed bush vines in a hot, dry climate
steps.explanation: Without irrigation, old vines give small crops.

steps.title: A revolution
steps.body: In the early 2000s, winemakers like Eben Sadie and Adi Badenhorst, then Chris and Andrea Mullineux, came to Swartland, drawn by old, forgotten vineyards. They made natural, low-intervention wines from old Chenin, Syrah and Grenache. In 2010, the Swartland Independent Producers set rules: no added yeast, no acidification, minimal sulphur, no new oak.

steps.prompt: Swartland's revival was led by young producers using old vineyards.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Swartland, the black land, lies north of Cape Town
It's hot and dry, with dry-farmed bush vines
A wave of young producers revived it from the 2000s
